title: Gas Station
directAnswer: Drive a circular route once, gaining gas[i] and spending cost[i] at each station. The brute force tries every start and simulates the loop in O(n²). The greedy does it in one pass: if total gas ≥ total cost a unique answer exists, and you find it by sweeping once — whenever your running tank dips below zero, the start can't be anywhere in the stretch you just covered, so reset start to the next station. O(n) time, O(1) space.

remember.pattern: Greedy circular feasibility — total check + reset-on-deficit
remember.formula:
if sum(gas) < sum(cost): return -1
start = 0; tank = 0
for i in range(n):
    tank += gas[i] - cost[i]
    if tank < 0:        # stretch [start..i] is doomed
        start = i + 1
        tank = 0
return start
rules: First settle existence: a solution exists **iff** `sum(gas) >= sum(cost)`. No total surplus → return `-1`.
Track a running **`tank`** of `gas[i] - cost[i]`. The instant it goes **negative**, every station from the current `start` through `i` is disqualified as a start.
On a deficit, **reset** `start = i + 1` and `tank = 0` — never re-test the stations you just abandoned.
You make exactly **one pass**; you never wrap around and re-simulate, because the total check already guarantees the surviving `start` completes the loop.
Use the **net** array `diff[i] = gas[i] - cost[i]` mentally — the question is purely about a circular running sum staying non-negative.
The answer is **unique** when it exists, so the first surviving `start` is *the* answer — no tie-breaking needed.
whenToUse: Circular / wrap-around route where you accumulate then spend a resource
You need a feasible *starting point*, not the full schedule
A running balance must stay non-negative across a loop
Total surplus guarantees a solution and you want to locate it in one sweep
antiSignals: Resource can be carried over multiple loops → it's not a single-circuit feasibility question
You must return *all* valid starts, not one → the uniqueness shortcut breaks
Costs depend on the order you visit (not fixed per edge) → model as a graph, not a linear sweep
Negative-only or fractional refuel rules → simulate or use a different model
remember.takeaway: Gas Station is the canonical 'circular running-sum' greedy: one global check decides existence, and a single reset-on-deficit sweep locates the unique start. The reset trick — 'the whole failing prefix is disqualified, jump past it' — is the same move you use in Maximum Subarray (Kadane) and Jump Game's frontier reset.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you separate the two questions — does a solution exist (a global sum check) versus where does it start (a local sweep) — and whether you can argue why a single left-to-right pass with a reset is enough rather than re-simulating every candidate.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Simulating from every start (O(n²)), or in the greedy resetting the tank but forgetting that the global `sum(gas) >= sum(cost)` check is what licenses returning the surviving start without re-wrapping.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Present the O(n²) simulation first, then split the problem: prove existence with the total comparison, and prove the start with the contradiction argument — if the tank dies at i starting from s, no station in [s, i] can be the answer.

problemStatement:
There are `n` gas stations along a **circular** route, where the amount of gas at the `i`-th station is `gas[i]`.

You have a car with an unlimited gas tank, and it costs `cost[i]` of gas to travel from the `i`-th station to its next `(i + 1)`-th station. You begin the journey with an empty tank at one of the gas stations.

Given two integer arrays `gas` and `cost`, return *the starting gas station's index if you can travel around the circuit once in the clockwise direction, otherwise return* `-1`.

If there exists a solution, it is **guaranteed to be unique**.
constraints: The answer is guaranteed to be unique if it exists
understanding: At each station you pick up gas[i] fuel and must pay cost[i] to reach the next station. Starting empty at some station, can you loop all the way around without the tank ever going negative? Return one valid starting index, or -1 if none exists. Only the net gas[i] − cost[i] per station matters.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the route truly circular — does the last station wrap back to the first?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. From station n−1 you pay cost[n−1] to return to station 0. That wrap-around is why a single linear scan needs justification.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the answer be ambiguous — multiple valid starts?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No, the problem guarantees a unique answer when one exists. That uniqueness is what lets us return the first surviving start without checking the rest.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if total gas exactly equals total cost?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Then a solution exists (surplus is zero, which is allowed — the tank may touch but never drop below zero across the full loop).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are gas and cost always non-negative?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, both are in [0, 10⁴], so each net diff is in [−10⁴, 10⁴]. No tricks with negative fuel pickups.

examples.explanation: Start at index 3: tank = 4. To 4: +5−1 = 8. To 0: +1−2 = 7. To 1: +2−3 = 6. To 2: +3−4 = 5. To 3: arrive with 5 ≥ 0 — full loop done.
Total gas 9 < total cost 10, so no starting station can complete the circuit.
Total gas 15 ≥ total cost 15, so a unique start exists; the sweep lands on index 4.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Existence is a global sum question; the start is a single sweep with a reset. Both halves are O(n).

approaches.name: Brute Force — Simulate From Every Start
approaches.whenToMention: Open with this to show you understand the mechanics of the circuit, then call out the O(n²) cost as the reason to look deeper.
hints: If you fix a starting station s, you can just drive: add gas[i] − cost[i] as you go and watch whether the tank ever drops below zero. What happens if you try this for every possible s?
For each start s in 0..n−1, walk all n stations using modular indexing (i + s) % n, accumulating the net. If it never goes negative across all n hops, s works.
Two nested loops: outer over the candidate start, inner over the n stations of the loop. Return the first s that survives; if none do, return −1.
approaches.complexityReasoning: For each of n candidate starts we simulate up to n stations, so O(n²) time in the worst case; we only keep a running tank, so O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
The most direct reading of the problem: pick a start, drive the full circle, and see if the tank ever goes negative. Repeat for every possible start and return the first one that survives the loop.

**Why this is the natural first attempt.** The problem describes a physical simulation — pick up gas, pay to move on — so the literal solution is to *run* that simulation. With no insight required, you fix a start `s`, use `(s + k) % n` to wrap around the circle, and keep a running `tank`. The first `s` whose tank stays non-negative for all `n` hops is an answer.

**Why the modular index matters.** The route is circular, so after the last station you must return to station 0. Using `(s + k) % n` for `k` from `0` to `n−1` visits every station exactly once *in driving order* starting from `s`, correctly modelling the wrap-around. Forgetting the modulo would simulate a straight line and miss the loop-closing cost.

**Why we don't ship this.** Each candidate start triggers a full `n`-station simulation, so the worst case is `n × n = n²` work. For `n = 10⁵` that's up to 10¹⁰ operations — far too slow. Worse, it throws away information: when a simulation from `s` dies partway, the brute force restarts from `s+1` from scratch, even though the failed stretch already told us those starts are hopeless. That wasted insight is exactly what the greedy reclaims.
approaches.insight: When a run starting at `s` fails at some station `j`, the brute force learns something it immediately discards: *no* station between `s` and `j` could have been a valid start either. Noticing that you can skip straight to `j + 1` instead of `s + 1` is the seed of the linear greedy — the same 'the whole failing prefix is dead' idea behind Kadane's reset.

dryRun.intro: Try each start; simulate all 5 hops with modular indexing. Return the first that never goes negative.

pitfalls: Forgetting the % n wrap — simulates a line and never closes the loop.
Resetting only to start+1 after a failure instead of recognising the whole failed stretch is dead (the missed optimisation).
Shipping O(n²) when n = 10⁵ guarantees a time-limit exceeded.

approaches.name: Greedy — Total Check + Reset On Deficit (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Frame it as 'two separate questions: does a start exist, and where is it' — then justify the reset with the contradiction argument.
hints: Split the problem. First: can ANY start work? That's a global question — compare total gas to total cost. If you're in deficit overall, no start can survive a full loop.
Now assume a start exists. Sweep left to right tracking a running tank of gas[i] − cost[i]. What does it mean if the tank goes negative somewhere between your current candidate start and station i?

If the tank dies at i, then NO station from the current start through i can be the answer — every one of them inherited an even worse running balance. So jump the candidate start to i + 1, reset the tank to 0, and keep sweeping. The surviving start is the answer.
approaches.complexityReasoning: One pass to compute the totals (or folded into the same loop) plus one sweep that resets in place — each station is touched a constant number of times, giving O(n) time and O(1) space (just two running integers).
approaches.explanation:
Separate the question into two cleaner ones. **Existence:** a full loop is possible if and only if `sum(gas) >= sum(cost)`, because completing the circle means the total fuel gained must cover the total fuel spent — the tank starts and ends empty-or-positive over a closed loop. If the global total is in deficit, return `-1` immediately. **Location:** assuming a start exists, sweep once with a running `tank`. Whenever `tank` drops below zero at station `i`, set `start = i + 1` and reset `tank = 0`. The `start` left standing at the end is the unique answer.

**Why total surplus guarantees a solution exists.** Over one full loop the net change is `sum(gas) − sum(cost)`. If that's negative, you burn more than you collect no matter where you begin, so `-1`. If it's `≥ 0`, the closed-loop net is non-negative, which is *exactly* the condition under which some rotation of the sequence keeps every prefix non-negative — a classic result about circular sequences. So the global check isn't just necessary, it's sufficient.

**Why a failing stretch disqualifies its entire span — the contradiction argument.** Suppose we start at `s` and the running tank first goes negative when we arrive at station `i` (so the sum of nets over `[s, i]` is negative). Claim: no station `t` with `s ≤ t ≤ i` can be a valid start. Here's the contradiction: when we started at `s`, our tank was non-negative at every station *before* `i` — in particular it was `≥ 0` when we reached any intermediate `t`. If instead we *began* at `t`, we'd start that same sub-journey from a tank of `0`, which is `≤` the tank we actually had arriving at `t` from `s`. So starting at `t` reaches `i` with an even *lower* balance than the run from `s` did — and that run already went negative. Therefore `t` fails too. Every candidate in `[s, i]` is dead, so the *earliest* station that could possibly work is `i + 1`. That is precisely why the reset jumps to `i + 1` rather than crawling forward one step.

**Why one pass with no re-wrap is enough.** The reset argument means the surviving `start` is never disqualified by anything to its left. Combined with the existence guarantee from the total check, the stretch from `start` to the end of the array accumulates a non-negative running sum, and the leftover deficit before `start` is exactly cancelled by the surplus after it when the loop wraps. So we never need to simulate the wrap-around explicitly — the global surplus certifies the wrap closes. That collapses the O(n²) re-simulation into a single linear sweep.

**Why this beats the brute force outright.** The brute force rediscovers each failure from scratch; the greedy uses each failure to *skip* an entire doomed prefix, and replaces per-start re-simulation with one global comparison. Same answer, O(n²) → O(n), O(1) space throughout.
approaches.insight: The unlock is realising these are two independent questions wearing one disguise: *whether* a start exists is global (sum of nets), and *which* start works is local (where does the running balance survive). The reset is the same move as Kadane's 'a negative running prefix can only hurt, so drop it' — here a negative running tank means the whole prefix since the last reset is unsalvageable, so you leap past all of it at once.

code.python:
def canCompleteCircuit(self, gas: list[int], cost: list[int]) -> int:
    total = 0
    tank = 0
    start = 0
    for i in range(len(gas)):
        diff = gas[i] - cost[i]
        total += diff
        tank += diff
        if tank < 0:
            start = i + 1
            tank = 0
    return start if total >= 0 else -1

java.explanation: total = global surplus (existence), tank = running balance since last reset (location), start = current candidate.
Only the net per station matters — gain minus cost to move on.
Accumulate the global surplus; its sign decides whether any start can work.
Stretch from start..i is doomed — by the contradiction argument no station in it can begin a successful loop.
Jump past the entire failed prefix, not just one step.
Surviving start is valid only if the global surplus is non-negative; otherwise no start completes the loop.

Net fuel change at station i.
Running balance died — the whole stretch since the last reset is unsalvageable.
Skip directly past the doomed prefix.
Return the surviving start when a loop is feasible overall, else -1.

edgeCases.behavior: total = (−1) + (−1) + 1 = −1 < 0, so regardless of the sweep's surviving start, the final check returns −1.
Single station: diff = 1, total = 1 ≥ 0, tank never negative → start stays 0, returns 0.
total = 2 + (−1) + (−1) = 0 ≥ 0; tank dips at i=2 (resets start=2 only if it goes negative) — surviving start completes the loop because surplus is exactly zero.

pitfalls: Returning start without the total >= 0 guard — gives a wrong index when no solution exists.
Resetting start but forgetting to also zero the tank — carries a phantom deficit into the next candidate.
Re-simulating the wrap-around explicitly — unnecessary once the total surplus certifies the loop closes.

commonMistakes: Simulating from every start in O(n²) instead of splitting into a global total check plus one sweep.
Returning the surviving start without first confirming sum(gas) ≥ sum(cost).
On a deficit, advancing start by only one step instead of jumping past the entire failed stretch to i + 1.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Returning start without the feasibility guard
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The sweep always leaves some surviving start, but it's only valid when the global surplus is non-negative. Skipping the total check returns a bogus index on infeasible inputs.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Forgetting to reset the tank on a deficit
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Advancing start but keeping the negative tank drags the old deficit into the new candidate's balance, corrupting every later comparison.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Crawling forward one station after a failure
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The contradiction argument proves the entire stretch [start, i] is dead, so moving start to i+1 is correct and O(n). Moving to start+1 and re-checking reintroduces the O(n²) brute force.

patternNote: Canonical circular running-sum greedy: a single global sum decides existence, and a reset-on-deficit sweep locates the unique start in one pass. Recognise it for wrap-around feasibility where a balance must stay non-negative; it shares its reset spirit with Kadane's Maximum Subarray and Jump Game's frontier.
